items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-16
items.q: When I went into Chicago I was sitting with Joe, Johnny Dots, Baby Dots and all of them good.

ctx.x: working with men that are better than you and I guess there was a time when there was someone better than you when you were awfully young.

All of my life in music and whatever happened to me right today comes from observing some of the musicians that were playing something. And I was always lucky to play with good musicians. When I went into Chicago I was sitting with Joe, Johnny Dots, Baby Dots and all of them good. Leo on piano and Joe Arroyo and Lauren at Horn. I said, why didn't we do it? Now, I went into the front set with Carol Dickerson's orchestra which was owned by Joe Glazer, my manager, and Joe Glazer and Joe Rollins who was called the…
I wouldn't listen to it. I've noticed you've talked a lot about Joe Oliver, and he must have been a tremendous influence.

items.title: Warren "Baby" Dodds Interview, 1958-05-31
items.q: And we had quite a healthy band. And you could tell when those guys come at the plane. Louis weighed 2.5 or 2.10.

ctx.x: Okay, it's going. Baby, since Joe Oliver isn't around anymore, I thought I'd ask you a few questions about Oliver and his band. At the time you knew him, that you played with him, how did you enjoy working with the band? Well, Bill, as far as the band's concerned, it was a swell band to work with. Everybody knew what they were doing, everybody was set with anything went off, everybody was ready. When did you join the Oliver band? Well, I joined the Oliver band by the year of 1921. I left the Stuckford's line in…

Okay, I guess it's going again. We might talk a little bit about Dutre too since he isn't here anymore to talk for himself. No, he was a comical guy. That was a comical man. Really comical. He was really comical. A man could bring a tail to tell you before you get off work, you got a tail to tell you when you get off work. After you get off work, you got one to tell you to keep your company all the way. If you stay out five hours, you got a tail to tell you for five hours. He was a great character. I was for the…

items.title: Louis Armstrong: Jazz Casual Interview, 1964-07-10
items.q: Now you spoke before about how they didn't have the drums. Baby Dodds just played Woodblocks.

ctx.x: It's one of them he made up for the Ginette record. When he started making records then he started being a writer. Yeah. And that stuff would come up later, you know. Would you rehearse that then in the studio before you recorded it? Well we'd rehearse that on the job, you know. Uh-huh. And then by the time we'd get to the studio all they'd do is cut it up and time it to, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. For no trouble at all, you know, to make them records, because they'd make one after another. It wasn't as particular as it…
Now you spoke before about how they didn't have the drums. Baby Dodds just played Woodblocks. Uh, that daughter's baby was there.

Yeah. Yeah. They didn't need him nowhere. They didn't use drums at all, right? No drums at all at that time. They were scared it would throw the needle off. I see. Yeah. So we got back good. But the only thing I have about those early recordings is that you didn't get that lead much. That's what I mean, because you couldn't do, you couldn't tell Joe what to do. Yeah. He was the boss. Yeah. Now those breaks that you two took on there. Well, yeah. Well, I put notes to his lead, whatever he made. I just, we didn't…
